title: Making a decision
objectives: Write comparisons with `<`, `<=`, `==` and `!=`, and read their boolean values.

screens.title: Follow the arrows
screens.prose: A trading program checks each new price against a stop level of £98.00. The circle with a question mark asks a yes-or-no question. Its answer picks the arrow to follow.
screens.question: The new price is £97.40. Tap the step the program carries out.

hints.text: Is 97.40 smaller than 98.00?
The question circle decides which arrow the program follows.
97.40 is below 98.00, so the answer is True. Follow the arrow marked True.

feedback.correct: 97.40 is below 98.00, so the answer is True and the program sells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer the question in the circle for 97.40, then follow that arrow.

byKey.hold: You followed the False arrow. 97.40 is less than 98.00, so the answer is True.

explain.text: The question 'below 98.00?' is `price < 98.00` in Python. Its answer is written `True` or `False`, and for £97.40 it is `True`. So the program follows the True arrow and sells.

screens.title: The same decision in Python
screens.prose:
Here is that flowchart written as Python. The last line prints `done`.

```python
price = 97.40
stop = 98.00
if price < stop:
    print("sell")
else:
    print("hold")
print("done")
```
screens.question: What does the program print?

options.why: You treated `print("done")` as part of the `if` block. It is not indented, so it runs whichever way the decision goes.
You ran both blocks. The `else` block runs only when the condition is `False`, and here it is `True`.
You took the `else` block. `97.40 < 98.00` is `True`, so the `if` block runs instead.

hints.text: Which lines are indented under `if`, and which under `else`?
The last line starts at the left edge, outside both blocks.
The condition is True, so the `if` block prints sell and the `else` block is skipped. Then the last line prints done.

feedback.correct: One branch runs, then the program carries on below.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the condition first, then follow only that branch, then the last line.

byKey.both: You ran both blocks. `else` runs only when the condition is `False`.

explain.text: `price < stop` is the **condition**. The indented lines under `if` are its **block**, run only when the condition is `True`; the `else` block runs only when it is `False`. The unindented last line runs either way.

screens.title: A comparison is a value
screens.prose:
A comparison can be stored in a variable, like a number.

```python
price = 101.25
stop = 98.00
below = price < stop
print(below)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected `below` to hold a price. It holds the answer to the comparison, which is `True` or `False`.
You read the sign the wrong way round. 101.25 is above 98.00, so `price < stop` is `False`.
`below` has no quotes, so it is a variable name. Python prints the value stored in it.

hints.text: Is 101.25 less than 98.00?
`below` stores whatever `price < stop` works out to.
101.25 is bigger than 98.00, so `price < stop` is False. That value is stored and printed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out `price < stop` first; that answer is what `below` holds.

explain.text: Python works out `price < stop` to `False` and stores it in `below`. `True` and `False` are the bool values you met with text, also called booleans. An `if` line only asks whether its condition's value is `True`.

screens.title: Exactly on the stop
screens.prose: Same program, same stop of £98.00. This time the price lands exactly on the stop.
screens.question: Tap the step the program carries out.

hints.text: Is 98.00 less than 98.00?
`<` means strictly less than. Equal is not less.
98.00 is not below itself, so `price < 98.00` is False. Follow the False arrow.

feedback.correct: 98.00 is not less than 98.00, so the program holds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether 98.00 is strictly less than 98.00.

byKey.sell: You read `<` as 'at or below'. A number is never less than itself, so `98.00 < 98.00` is `False`.

explain.text: `98.00 < 98.00` is `False`, so the program holds. To sell at the stop as well, the test would be `price <= stop`, read 'less than or equal to'. Prices that land exactly on a level are where these tests differ.

screens.title: Three ways out
screens.prose: The program now also takes profit above £110.00. A False answer to the first question leads to a second question.
screens.question: The price is £112.50. Tap every circle the program passes through.

hints.text: Answer the first question for 112.50. Which arrow does that give?
112.50 is not below 98.00, so the program moves on to the second question.
The first answer is False, so the program asks the second question. 112.50 is above 110.00, so it takes profit. Tap both questions and take profit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at the first question and follow one arrow at a time.

byKey.sell: You took the True arrow at the first question. 112.50 is not below 98.00, so that answer is False.
byKey.hold: You took the False arrow at the second question. 112.50 is above 110.00, so the answer is True.
byKey.q1: Every price passes through the first question. Tap it too.
byKey.q2: The first answer is False, so the program asks the second question before acting. Tap it too.
byKey.take: Follow the second question's True arrow to the step the program carries out.

explain.text: The first answer is `False`, so the program asks the second question, and that answer is `True`. In Python the second question is written `elif`, short for 'else if'. The program asks its questions in order and acts at the first `True`.

screens.title: The first True wins
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You picked the branch that fits best. Python takes the first `True` condition, and `change > 2` comes first.
You ran every branch whose condition holds. Once one branch runs, the rest of the chain is skipped.
You took the `else` branch. 6.5 is above 2, so the first condition is `True`.

hints.text: Which condition does Python ask first?
On the flowchart, the first question's True arrow leaves before the second question is asked.
`change > 2` is True for 6.5, so `up` prints. The chain ends there, and `change > 5` is never asked.

feedback.correct: The first True condition wins, and the rest are skipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask the conditions in order and stop at the first True one.

byKey.best: You picked the branch that fits best. Python stops at the first `True` condition, which is `change > 2`.

explain.text: `change > 2` is `True` for 6.5, so `up` prints and the chain ends. The `elif change > 5` question is never asked. To reach `big up`, put the stricter test first: `change > 5`, then `change > 2`.

screens.title: One equals sign or two
screens.prose:
A signal is stored as text, and the program should send an order when it is `"buy"`.

```python
signal = "buy"
if signal = "buy":
    print("send order")
```
screens.question: What happens when you run it?

options.why: You read `=` as 'is equal to'. In Python one `=` stores a value, and storing is not a question, so `if` cannot use it.

options.text: Python stops with a `SyntaxError` before running any line.
It prints nothing, because the test fails.
options.why: You expected a False answer. Python never asks the question: it rejects the line while reading the program.

options.text: It stores `"buy"` in `signal` again, then prints `send order`.
options.why: Some languages do that. Python refuses a single `=` inside a condition, so nothing is stored or printed.

hints.text: What does a single `=` do on its own line, such as `signal = "buy"`?
One `=` stores a value. Comparing needs a different symbol.
Python reads the whole program before running it. `if signal = "buy":` is not a valid line, so it stops with a SyntaxError and runs nothing.

feedback.correct: One `=` stores a value; two, `==`, compare.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what one `=` means in Python, and whether `if` can use that.

byKey.runs: You read `=` as 'is equal to'. That is `==` in Python; one `=` stores a value, so this line is rejected.
byKey.stores: That happens in some other languages. Python rejects a single `=` inside a condition.

explain.text: Python stops before running anything: `SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?`. One `=` means 'store this value under this name'; asking 'are these equal?' takes two. The fix is `if signal == "buy":`.

screens.title: Up, down or flat
screens.prose:
Now write a decision yourself. The `def` and `return` lines are given: they let the tests try your lines on many changes. A later level explains them.

Set `word` to `"up"` when `change` is above 0, `"down"` when it is below 0, and `"flat"` when it is exactly 0.
screens.question: Write the `if`, `elif` and `else` lines inside `label`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each calls `label` with one price change and compares the word exactly, so `"Up"` or `"up "` fails.

hints.text: Three outcomes need three branches: `if`, one `elif` and `else`.
Your lines go between the two given lines, indented by 4 spaces. Each branch's own line is indented 4 more.
Write `if change > 0:` then `word = "up"` indented under it. Do the same with `elif change < 0:` and `"down"`. Finish with `else:` and `"flat"`.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed, including the change of exactly 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Try a change of exactly 0: neither `> 0` nor `< 0` holds, so `else` must catch it.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check the colon at the end of each `if`, `elif` and `else` line, and the indents.

screens.title: The shape of a decision
screens.prose:
You followed arrows, then wrote them as Python. Each condition is a boolean, $\texttt{True}$ or $\texttt{False}$; Python runs the block under the first $\texttt{True}$ one and skips the rest.

```python
if price < stop:        # asked first
    action = "sell"
elif price > target:    # asked if first False
    action = "take profit"
else:                   # all were False
    action = "hold"
```

Comparisons: `<` `<=` `>` `>=`, `==` (equal) and `!=` (not equal).
screens.question: Which line asks whether `qty` is zero?

options.why: One `=` stores a value. Python rejects it inside a condition with a SyntaxError.
That compares with the text `"0"`. A number never equals text, so this is always `False`.
`!=` means 'not equal', so this asks the opposite question.

feedback.correct: Two equals signs ask the question.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the comparison that asks 'is equal to' with a number.

explain.text: `==` compares and gives a boolean; `=` stores. The number `0` and the text `"0"` are different values, so they are never equal.

screens.title: A stop-loss
screens.prose: You bought shares at £104.00 and set a stop-loss at £98.00. The desk's rule: sell when a price is strictly below the stop, otherwise hold. Your check runs on every new price.
screens.question: Complete `stop_check` so it returns `"sell"` or `"hold"`.

widget.starter:
def stop_check(price, stop):
    action = "hold"
    # set action to "sell" if price is below stop
    
    return action
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests, each with a price and a stop. A price exactly on the stop must hold.

hints.text: `action` already starts as `"hold"`. When should it change?
One `if` is enough. No `else` is needed, because `action` already holds the other answer.
Add `if price < stop:` and, indented under it, `action = "sell"`.

feedback.correct: Your stop-loss sells below £98.00 and holds at or above it.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check a price exactly on the stop: the rule says hold.

byKey.test-2: A price exactly on the stop must hold. Use `<`, not `<=`.

explain.text:
Starting `action` at `"hold"` means one `if` covers both outcomes. Real stop orders differ on whether they fire at the level itself. That choice is exactly `<` against `<=`.

```python
def stop_check(price, stop):
    action = "hold"
    if price < stop:
        action = "sell"
    return action
```

ideas: A comparison such as `price < stop` is a boolean value: `True` or `False`.
`if`, `elif` and `else` ask their conditions in order and run only the block under the first `True` one.
Indented lines belong to the block above them; an unindented line runs whichever branch was taken.

formula.name: A decision
formula.note: At most one branch runs: the first whose condition is True, else the `else` block.

summary.trap: One `=` stores a value; two, `==`, compare. `if x = 0:` is a SyntaxError.

quiz.prose:
```python
qty = 100
if qty >= 100:
    print("large")
else:
    print("small")
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You read `>=` as `>`. `>=` includes equal, so `100 >= 100` is `True`.
You ran both blocks. `else` runs only when the condition is `False`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out `100 >= 100` first.

explain.text: `>=` reads 'greater than or equal to', so `100 >= 100` is `True` and `large` prints. The `else` block is skipped.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You went to the last branch that fits. Python takes the first `True` condition, and `pnl < -200` comes before `pnl < 0`.
You ran every branch whose condition holds. After one branch runs, the rest of the chain is skipped.
You expected nothing without an `else`. Here the second condition is `True`, so its branch runs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask the conditions in order and stop at the first True one.

explain.text: `pnl > 0` is `False`. `pnl < -200` is `True` for −250, so `big loss` prints and the chain ends. With no `else`, a P&L of exactly 0 would print nothing.

quiz.prose:
```python
stop = 98.00
price = 98.00
print(price == stop, price < stop)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You treated `<` as 'at or below'. 98.00 is not less than itself.
You expected `==` to fail. The two prices are the same value, so `==` gives `True`.
`print` shows the comparisons' answers, which are booleans, not the prices.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each comparison on its own.

explain.text: `price == stop` is `True` because both are 98.0. `price < stop` is `False` because nothing is less than itself. `print` shows both booleans on one line, with a space between them.

quiz.prose: Python reads every line before it runs any.
quiz.question: Which line does Python reject with a `SyntaxError`?

options.why: This is the correct way to ask 'is `pnl` equal to 0?'.
`<=` is a valid comparison: 'less than or equal to'.
This is allowed. The right side is a comparison, and its boolean is stored in `flat`.

feedback.correct: A single `=` cannot be a condition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a single `=` where Python expects a question.

explain.text: `if pnl = 0:` tries to store inside a condition, so Python rejects it. `flat = pnl == 0` is fine: `==` compares, then `=` stores the boolean in `flat`.
